scenario.briefing: A stock import accepts quantities from a text file. Invalid rows must report why they failed without crashing the importer.

title: Typed errors at the input boundary
summary: Throw specific parse errors instead of trapping, then repair a report that turns every failure into zero.

objectives.description: Throw typed errors from a validation function.
Find a handler that hides invalid input.
Choose the call that propagates an error.

hints: An enum that conforms to Error can name each failure.
guard let converts the text safely.
Throw a different case for non-positive values.
Use do/catch when the caller must see which error happened.

misconceptions.description: Force unwrapping the result of Int(text).
misconceptions.testDescription: Invalid text throws the notANumber case.
misconceptions.feedback: Int(text)! traps on non-numeric input. guard let turns that absence into a typed throw the caller can handle.

misconceptions.description: Believing try? preserves the error for the caller.
misconceptions.feedback: try? converts any thrown error into nil. Use try inside a throwing function or do/catch when the caller needs the failure.

misconceptions.description: Logging an import failure and continuing with zero.
misconceptions.feedback: A log line is not a recovery policy. Re-throw, return a failure result, or skip and report the row explicitly.

misconceptions.description: Reporting every failure as the same error case.
misconceptions.diagnostic: Throwing notANumber for a negative value so the caller cannot distinguish syntax from range.
misconceptions.feedback: Separate syntax failures from range failures. The caller can retry a missing value, but a negative quantity needs a different response.

sections.title: Errors are typed values
sections.body: An enum conforming to Error names each failure: enum QuantityError: Error { case notANumber; case notPositive }. A throwing function writes throws after its parameter list, and every failure leaves through throw. The compiler checks that callers use try, try?, or do/catch.

sections.title: Validate at the boundary
sections.body: Convert text once, then check the domain rule. guard let value = Int(text) else { throw QuantityError.notANumber } makes the syntax failure explicit. A second guard rejects zero and negative values. Keeping validation in one small function gives tests a clear contract.

sections.title: Choose a recovery policy
sections.body: try? is appropriate only when every failure has the same harmless outcome. try! asserts that failure is impossible and traps otherwise. do/catch preserves the specific error, and a throwing caller can propagate it with try. Swift Package Manager runs the suite with swift test, while swiftc compiles a single file.

steps.title: The zero that hides a typo
steps.prompt: An import of 200 rows reports success with a total of zero. Select the faulty instruction and the correct repair.
hints: The parser probably told the caller something useful.
try? turns every thrown error into nil.
nil is then flattened to zero by the default.
Use do/catch and report the specific error.

fixes.label: Use do/catch, print the specific error, and stop the row.
Use try! so the error cannot be ignored.
Keep try? and return zero without a log line.

steps.explanation: try? discards which error occurred, and ?? 0 turns every failure into a plausible-looking total. do/catch keeps the failure visible. try! would crash the importer instead of reporting the row.

steps.title: Propagate or erase
steps.prompt: Inside a throwing import function, which call passes a parse failure to its caller?
hints: A throwing function can forward an error with try.
try? converts the error to nil.
A bare call does not satisfy the compiler.

quiz.prompt: Inside a throwing import function, which call passes a parse failure to its caller?
quiz.explanation: try propagates the thrown error from a throwing function. try? returns nil, try! traps, and a plain call does not compile.
